_comment: Pattern corpus for cadence.py. Every tell carries a tier, and the tier says how the hit is handled, not how hard it fires. What each tier means is in ../references/tiers.md; this file is the enumeration and that file never lists members. Patterns are Python regex, matched case-insensitively. `swap` is a starting suggestion for the model, never an automatic substitution. This file ships no `house` tells: a repository's own house rules arrive through --overlay.

tiers.house: Barred by a house rule in this repository's conventions folder. Not a detection heuristic and not a judgment call. Remove it.
tiers.forensic: No human writer produces this. It is model leakage or template residue. Remove it.
tiers.strict: Heavily machine-associated and bad style regardless of who wrote it. Rewrite it, and say what you did.
tiers.aesthetic: Machine-associated but also normal in good human writing. Report it, decide in context, and leave it alone when it is doing work.

_preserve_comment: Words a project uses precisely, blanked before any tell is matched so a domain term is never reported as brochure register. Whole-word and case-insensitive. Empty here: a repository adds its own words through an --overlay file.

tells.note: Model tool-call artifact pasted through into the draft.
Search-tool call leakage.
Numbered citation residue from a tool response. Markdown footnotes are not this and are not matched.

tells.pattern: \bas of my (last update|knowledge cutoff|training cutoff|last training)[^.]*\.
tells.note: Delete the whole sentence. A person has no training cutoff.
Delete the whole sentence.
Assistant register. Delete the whole sentence.
Delete the whole sentence.
Unfilled template slot. Ask the author for the value; never invent one.
Unfilled date slot.
Draft scaffolding that was never removed. `todo:` carries no trailing boundary, because a colon is not a word character.

Dickinson and Didion lean on it, and so does a lot of generated prose. A repository whose house rules bar it promotes this id to `house` in its overlay. Where it stays, read the density: one in a page is punctuation, one per paragraph is a habit worth breaking with a period, comma or colon.
Normal in a chat message or a social post, a tell in an essay or a report heading. A repository whose house rules bar it promotes this id to `house` in its overlay.
It needs a modifier key or an autocorrect to appear, so outside a numeric range it usually arrived from a model or a word processor. A numeric range is the case where it is doing work.
Slide glyph standing in for a verb. Fires inside tables and diagram captions too, where it is usually right.
Say use, or name the thing being used.
Use.
Name the action instead.
Brochure register.
The most-cited generated-text marker in circulation.
Fine when something is literally being steered.
Brochure register, unless something is literally locked.

Brochure register in the inflected verb. The bare noun is a domain term in some projects, which is what `preserve` is for. `harnesses` is kept even though it is also a plural noun, which is rarer than the verb.
Brochure register.

Enumerating connectors.

tells.pattern: \b(in conclusion|in summary|to summarize|to sum up|in essence|all in all|at the end of the day)\b
tells.note: The closing move that restates the opening. Stop at the last real point instead.
Paragraph-initial summary adverb.
Empty topic-shifting phrase.
The generated-essay opening.
Dated the moment it was written.

tells.pattern: \b(game[- ]?chang(er|ing)|deep dive|move the needle|needle[- ]moving|paradigm shift|pivotal moment|a testament to|best[- ]in[- ]class|next[- ]level|state[- ]of[- ]the[- ]art|cutting[- ]edge)\b
tells.note: Consultancy filler with no human defense.
Quantity words that refuse to give a number. Give the number.

tells.pattern: \bit('s| is) (worth noting|important to note|essential to note|crucial to note)\b
tells.note: If it is worth noting, note it.
Passive throat-clearing.

tells.pattern: \b(could potentially|may potentially|might possibly|it seems that|arguably one of)\b
tells.note: Two hedges on one claim. Pick one, or make the claim.
The It's not X, it's Y construction. Rewrite as two statements and check the meaning survived.
Same construction, negated form.
Balanced correlative, rare in speech.
The addresses-everyone construction. Pick the reader.

tells.pattern: (?im)^[\s>*\-"']*(in today'?s |have you ever |most people don'?t (realize|know)|here'?s a hard truth|let me tell you about |picture this|imagine a world)
tells.note: Generated-post openers.

tells.pattern: \b(i'?m (excited|thrilled|delighted|proud) to (announce|share)|honou?red to be|delighted to be featured|excited to share)\b
tells.note: Reads as a press release. Lead with the concrete thing.

tells.pattern: (?i)(what (do|are) you think\??|what'?s your (take|thoughts?)|thoughts\?|agree or disagree\?|let me know (in the comments|your thoughts)|tag someone|drop a comment|smash the like)
tells.note: Engagement bait. Ask something only this piece could prompt, or close without asking.

tells.pattern: \b(let that sink in|read that again|sound familiar\?|here'?s the (thing|kicker|catch)|plot twist)\b
tells.note: Manufactured beats.
Generated-explainer openers.

tells.pattern: \bi hope (this|you)[^.?!\n]{0,40}(finds you well|are doing well|are well)\b|\b(just )?wanted to (reach out|check in|follow up|touch base)\b
tells.note: The best-known email tells. Neither says anything.

tells.pattern: \b(i'?d love to|happy to chat|more than happy to|circle back|touch base|looking forward to hearing|does that work for you\?)\b
tells.note: Warmth asserted on the writer's behalf.
A one-word rhetorical question as its own paragraph. Fine once in a piece with a voice; a pattern when it recurs.

A three-item series, with or without the conjunction. The lookaheads keep appositives and relative clauses out. Lincoln, Caesar and Churchill all used it: one or two is rhythm, one per paragraph is a template.
Normal in science and often the right choice. Report the rate; do not sweep.

Perfect and modal passives. `has walked` is active and is not counted. A simple passive with no auxiliary, `was written`, is not counted either, so read the rate as a floor rather than the passive rate. Over roughly 10 percent of clauses starts to flatten agency.
Huber 1964 and all of epidemiology use it precisely. Keep it where it means resistant to outliers; cut it where it means good.
Claims a set without enumerating it. Name the members, or the count.
Every one has a real writer defending it. Cut only where it is doing no work.
Importance asserted rather than demonstrated. Sometimes it genuinely is critical.
Word and Pages produce these, so does the New Yorker. Only a tell alongside others.
